paras: The attempted lynching of Sam Bailey was an armed pursuit of a Black furnace worker by a crowd of white men at North Birmingham, Alabama, on 10 October 1903, after he resisted arrest by an officer. Bailey escaped into the woods after an exchange of gunfire, and no report of his capture was found. The Birmingham Age-Herald wrote that a lynching "was only averted by his escaping from the mob," and a wire dispatch carried the chase to papers from Georgia to Arizona.
Bailey worked at the furnace at North Birmingham. According to the Age-Herald, Officer Lark Strong went to arrest him on the afternoon of 10 October for carrying concealed weapons.

The Age-Herald's account, drawn from the officers, said Bailey drew a pistol as Strong approached and fired a shot that tore the cuff from Strong's coat without injuring him. In the struggle that followed, Bailey used the gun as a club and knocked Strong stunned into a ditch, then retreated into his house as Deputy Sheriff W. Coles arrived. Strong recovered and, with the deputy, raised a crowd armed with pistols and shotguns that advanced on the house.

Shots were exchanged between Bailey and the crowd, and he escaped through the back door, "hotly pursued by the armed citizens who were determined to get him, dead or alive." During the chase he fired at Strong and at pursuers named as McCurry, L. Prost and J. Russell, and McCurry fired back with a shotgun. The wire dispatch described a "mob of white men" firing as they ran down the street and said more than 100 shots were fired, with several men left with bullet holes in their clothing.

Bailey was lost sight of at Baker's store in Jonesville, and the search went on until dark. A posse was then organized to search the woods, and the dispatch said that if sighted he was "almost sure to be shot," since he reportedly swore he would not be taken alive.

Strong was the only person reported injured, with a wound on his right cheek bone from the blow. Marshal Cole said he was satisfied Bailey had been hit by McCurry's shotgun, though the same report described the return fire as "apparently without effect." Chief Cole expected an arrest that night, but later briefs as late as 23 October still described a posse searching the woods, and no report of a capture, trial or death was found.

The Birmingham Age-Herald gave the story a long local report under the headlines "NEGRO DESPERADO SHOOTS AT OFFICER" and "MISCREANT STILL AT LARGE." It called the pursuers "armed citizens" and mentioned the averted lynching without comment on the crowd.

The wire dispatch from Birmingham ran on 11 October in the Montgomery Advertiser as "NEGRO SHOT DEPUTY" and in the Savannah Morning News as "ALABAMA NEGRO PURSUED BY MOB." Shorter versions appeared the same day in the Indianapolis Journal ("MAN HUNT IN ALABAMA"), the Saint Paul Globe and the Wichita Daily Eagle, and on 12 October in the Arizona Republican. The wire led with the wounding of the deputy and treated the mob's intent to shoot Bailey on sight as plain news.

By mid-October the story had shrunk to single sentences in news-summary columns in Wisconsin and Mississippi weeklies, one of which named the officer "Jack Strong." All the coverage found came from white papers, and none gave Bailey's own version of events.

The Age-Herald said Bailey's shot missed Strong and that the officer's wound came from a blow, while the wire dispatch said Strong was "shot and wounded" and a Mississippi brief said simply that he "was shot." The local paper placed the encounter in the afternoon, while the dispatch said it happened at night; every account of the shooting comes from the officers' and pursuers' side.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Sam Bailey
bases: An armed crowd raised by officers fired on and chased Bailey, and the local paper called it an averted lynching (A1, A2).
The local Age-Herald (A1) and the independent Birmingham wire dispatch (A2, A3) agree on the arrest attempt, the armed pursuit and Bailey's escape.

accounts.label: Local paper, officers' account
accounts.gist: Bailey fired at Strong when approached for carrying a concealed weapon, then clubbed him with the gun; Strong and Deputy Coles raised an armed crowd that besieged his house and chased him, and a lynching was 'only averted by his escaping'.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Strong was shot and wounded during an arrest; Bailey fled with a mob of white men firing after him, emptied two revolvers into the crowd, and escaped to the woods after more than 100 shots; a posse expected to shoot him on sight.

framing.detail: The Age-Herald headlined Bailey as a 'NEGRO DESPERADO' and 'MISCREANT', called the pursuers 'armed citizens', and noted the averted lynching without criticism of the crowd.
Wire versions led with the shooting of the deputy ('NEGRO SHOT DEPUTY', 'NEGRO SHOOTS SHERIFF AND ESCAPES A MOB') and reported the mob pursuit and the likelihood he would be shot as plain news.
Small-town papers reduced the story to a one-sentence brief in news-summary columns.

versions.value: Bailey's shot only tore the cuff of Strong's coat; Strong was injured by a blow from the gun used as a club (wound on right cheek bone)

conflicts.note: The local Age-Herald gives the most detailed account; the wire's 'shot and wounded' is likely a compression.
Two papers agree on Lark; 'Jack' appears only in a one-line brief.
The chase continued until dark in the Age-Herald account.

versions.value: Several shots at the house, then individual shots at named pursuers, returned by the crowd
